title: Microframe Scheduler & Tool Tunneling — PRD draft
content:
Purpose and scope:

This is an exploratory PRD sketch proposing a combined runtime and SDK convention for reducing end-to-end latency and increasing predictability for real-time tool-driven flows on Hosted API. The two tightly coupled ideas are: (1) a microframe scheduler in the server runtime that slices incremental outputs into small, labeled frames optimized for tool identification and quick client consumption, and (2) a tool tunneling adapter in SDKs that makes tool calls first-class, fast-path operations with typed partial responses and resumable handshakes.

Why this matters (problem statement):
- Customers building interactive, tool-heavy flows (search + tool lookup, multi-step agent loops, embedding-assisted lookups) experience high tail latency and complex client-side glue to reconcile partial text output with tool triggers.
- Existing streaming contracts either emit opaque deltas or monolithic structured blobs late in the stream; both force clients to buffer or run heuristics for tool detection.
- SDKs today surface streaming as raw chunks; teams end up duplicating parsing, backoff/hedging, and session-resume logic, increasing developer friction and bug surface.

Goals (what success looks like):
- 90th percentile tool invocation latency reduced by 35% for benchmarked agent flows compared to current streaming baseline.
- SDKs provide a single ergonomic primitive for declarative tool invocation and partial structured-result consumption.
- Graceful degradation: when structured frames are delayed, clients can fallback to text heuristics without corruption.
- Backwards-compatible: existing clients should continue to work with minimal changes.

Non-goals:
- End-to-end agent orchestration orchestration features (we do not build a full agent runtime on the platform).
- Replacing function-calling fundamentals (we extend, not remove, current tool-calling semantics).

Primary personas:
- Product engineers embedding interactive assistants in web/mobile apps who need predictable action triggers and low perceived latency.
- SDK maintainers who want a minimal surface area to implement advanced streaming semantics.
- Platform reliability engineers concerned with burst behavior and tail-latency of streaming pipelines.

High-level approach (two axes):
1) Server-side microframe scheduler:
   - The runtime will segment generated output into microframes: small, labeled tokens-of-interest (think: frames ~20-120ms worth of tokens under typical throughput). Each frame includes minimal metadata: sequence id, schemaVersion, frameType (text, tool-signal, tool-result, checkpoint), optional checksum.
   - Frames are aggressively prioritized by the scheduler: tool-signal frames are flushed before large narrative frames to reduce detection latency. A priority-queue routes frames to client connections; non-critical frames can be batched.
   - Built-in lightweight validation ensures partial structured payloads can be parsed without the full preceding context (typed segments are self-describing).

2) SDK tool tunneling adapter:
   - SDKs expose a new primitive: client.invokeStream(request, {tools: [..], streamingSchema: 'microframe-v1'}) which returns an async iterator of typed frames. The iterator yields objects with shape {frame_type, payload, seq, resume_token?} (conveyed over wire as compact JSON or ndjson).
   - Provide high-level helpers: .onToolSignal(cb), .collectPartial(schema), .resumeFrom(token). These helpers hide backoff, hedging, idempotency and resume semantics.
   - The adapter implements local, optimistic tool prefetch for frequently used tools and speculative invocation for low-cost tools (configurable via SDK options).

Structured schema and versioning:
- We define a small canonical schema microframe-v1.0 with a vocabulary for frame types and a compact typed payload encoding:
   - text: incremental text delta (prefix-only, no need for reassembly beyond seq).
   - tool-signal: identifies a tool should be invoked; payload contains {tool_id, confidence, minimal_args_schema}.
   - tool-result: partial or final result from a tool; payload contains typed fields and resume_token when the tool result is streamable.
   - checkpoint: lightweight marker for resuming or reconciling client state.
- Backward compatibility: servers will include a compatibility header indicating support for microframe-v1 and a fallback path that emits traditional streaming tokens for older clients.

Example flow (simplified):
1. Client calls invokeStream with tools [search, calculator].
2. Server sends frames: 
   - seq 1: text -> "Drafting answer: "
   - seq 2: tool-signal -> {tool_id: "search", confidence: 0.92, minimal_args: {q: "query snippet"}}
   - client SDK receives tool-signal and can immediately call the registered tool adapter with minimal args.
   - seq 3: text -> "Found result, synthesizing..." (lower priority)
   - seq 4: tool-result -> {tool_id: "search", items: [...], partial: true, resume_token: "tkn:..."}
3. If network interrupts, client can call .resumeFrom(last_seen_token) which establishes a reconnection handshake; server replays checkpoint frames and subsequent microframes until the stream is complete.

Resumability and idempotency:
- Each microframe can carry an optional resume_token when the server or tool expects long-running results. The SDK uses resume_token to request missing frames after reconnect and to avoid duplicate tool side-effects (platform enforces idempotency tokens for tool invocations).

Scheduler policies and SLOs:
- Default policy: prioritize tool-signal frames if their projected tool-invocation confidence is above 0.7 and estimated tool latency > 50ms.
- Rate limit interaction: microframes contain a budget hint so clients and intermediate proxies can throttle gracefully without losing tool triggers.
- SLO targets: 95th percentile microframe delivery within 120ms on the hosted tier for regions with <50ms round trip. These will be verified in dedicated benchmarks.

SDK ergonomics details:
- Low friction surface: a single streaming iterator is the only new primitive; helpers are opt-in. This minimizes cognitive load for simple use cases.
- Declarative tooling: developers declare tool shapes and side-effect policies when constructing a client to ensure the platform can enforce idempotency and telemetry. Example: new Client({tools: [{id: 'search', idempotency: 'query-hash'}]})
- On-device fallbacks: mobile SDKs should expose a compact fallback mode that returns the first tool-signal as a blocking result (for constrained networks), optionally switching to full streaming once connectivity improves.
- Diagnostics: SDK records microframe latency histograms, sequence gaps, and resume attempts to the telemetry pipeline. SDKs expose a debug flag to log raw frames in development builds.

Operational concerns and mitigation:
- Increased concurrency: prioritizing tool-signal frames may increase small-packet load. We'll implement adaptive batching for low priority frames and TCP-level optimizations.
- Security: microframe tool-signal payloads must not leak sensitive context. We enforce redaction rules and KMS-bound signatures for tool invocation arguments used across account boundaries.
- Failure modes: define explicit client-visible frame types for tool-failure, tool-timeout, and platform-fallback so clients can render graceful UX.

Migration and rollout plan:
1. Proto rollout behind feature flag. Launch microframe-v1 as opt-in for specific developer orgs.
2. SDK release: beta with JS and mobile (iOS/Android) offering adapter primitives and sample integrations.
3. Telemetry/benchmarks: instrument canaries with agent-like prompts; compare latency and correctness versus baseline streams.
4. Progressive enablement: flip default for new orgs, keep existing orgs on legacy streaming unless they opt in.

Success metrics and monitoring:
- Latency: 50th/90th/95th percentile time from server generation to SDK onToolSignal callback.
- Correctness: percentage of tool-signal frames that map to a correct tool invocation within client.
- Reliability: resume success rate after transient interruption.
- Developer feedback: adoption rate of SDK helpers and qualitative feedback from partner integrations.

Open questions and trade-offs:
- How aggressively should server speculative tool-signal detection be tuned to avoid spurious triggers? (tradeoff: lower latency vs false positives)
- Should the resume_token be universally applied or only for long-running tool-results?
- How to balance telemetry privacy vs actionable diagnostics in third-party tool integrations?

Implementation notes (engineering pointers):
- Services touched: serving-runtime (microframe generation), streaming-router (priority queue), api-gateway (compat headers), sdk libs (invokeStream + helpers), telemetry pipeline (new microframe metrics).
- Minimal data representation: ndjson with short keys for wire efficiency; binary protobuf optional for high-volume paths.
- Backwards compatibility: gateway should translate microframe-v1 frames to legacy token streams for older clients; this will be rate-limited to avoid double work.

Appendix A — Minimal example frames (ndjson lines):
{"seq":1,"frame_type":"text","payload":"Drafting answer: "}
{"seq":2,"frame_type":"tool-signal","payload":{"tool_id":"search","confidence":0.92,"args":{"q":"price of redwood inference"}}}
{"seq":3,"frame_type":"tool-result","payload":{"tool_id":"search","items":[{"title":"Redwood Inference — pricing"}],"partial":true}}
{"seq":4,"frame_type":"checkpoint","payload":{"token":"chk:abc123"}}

Appendix B — Developer example (JS pseudo):
const it = client.invokeStream({prompt: p}, {tools: [search], schema: 'microframe-v1'});
for await (const frame of it) {
  if (frame.frame_type === 'tool-signal') {
    // SDK helper for invoking registered adapter and attaching idempotency token
    client.toolAdapter.invoke(frame.payload.tool_id, frame.payload.args, {idempotency: frame.seq});
  }
  if (frame.frame_type === 'tool-result') {
    renderPartialResult(frame.payload);
  }
}

Notes for follow-up:
- Schedule cross-team whiteboard with serving-runtime and SDK leads to validate wire encoding and edge cases.
- Prepare initial benchmark harness: three agent prompts, two tools each, measure 95th percentile tool-signal latency.
- Draft a short migration guide for customers using existing streaming SDKs.

This is intentionally a sketch — needs concrete wire spec, resume-token format, and SDK API signatures before implementation.
